Before a doctor can submit a prior authorization, they need to check if the patient's insurance is even active. They need to know the copay, the coinsurance, the deductible status, all of it. Because patients need to be charged correctly and they deserve to know what they're paying upfront.

This isn't optional. It's a required step in the workflow.
Most clinics pull this data from clearinghouses like @Availity . Real time eligibility verification, benefits information, coverage details. It's all there. But there's a problem.

@Availity doesn't have an API.

Which means staff have to log into the portal manually. Search for each patient. Pull the eligibility data. Copy it into their system. Then move on to the next patient and do it all over again.

When you're running 30, 40, 50 patients a day, this adds up fast. One clinic told us their front desk was spending close to 2 hours every day just on eligibility checks. Not answering calls, not scheduling appointments, not helping patients. Just logging into Availity and copying information. That's almost 10 hours a week. Per person. On something that should take seconds.

This demo shows what we at @Optexity  built to fix it. You send patient details to Optexity, and it handles the entire @Availity lookup automatically. What comes back is structured data you can actually use. Member status, total deductible, remaining deductible, PCP copay, specialist copay. All formatted and ready to plug into whatever system you're running.

@Availity doesn't offer an API. But now you have one anyway. The data flows out automatically, and your team never has to touch the portal again.

We're in production now serving companies across the US Healthcare System. If your team is still doing eligibility checks manually, you can start using Optexity today.

Open source. Free to use. Reach out if you want help getting set up.

•Package your model in the supported format.

6.Act as a Reputer or verifier

•Opt into verification tasks where available.

•Compare model outputs to ground truth after the event window.

•Record your votes and follow dispute procedures if they exist.

http://7.Run a validator or node (advanced)

http://8.Report issues and feedback

•Use the project’s GitHub issues for reproducible bug reports.

How rewards and reputation move on testnet

1.Early participation gives reputation signals.

2.Accurate submissions improve model and contributor ranking.

3.Validators and Reputers build credibility for mainnet allocation.

4.Track your leaderboard position and accuracy metrics.

Best practices

1.Start small, scale submissions after you confirm format.

2.Timestamp and archive every request and response.

3.Never use mainnet keys or funds on testnet.

http://4.Read scoring rules before submitting at scale.

Metrics to track

1.Submission accuracy.

2.Latency from inference request to recorded result.

3.Reward rate per task.

4.Leaderboard rank trends over time.

2.Submitting too late in the topic window.

The thread is centered around drugmaker gamesmanship and rent seeking behavior. 

Don’t get me wrong - I was critical, but I didn’t intend to come across as ‘anti’ drug or ‘anti’ innovation, just to point out rampant problems with drug pricing specifically and how the government wants to solve them.

At the end of the day I think we can agree that we just want market-driven, rational drug pricing. I’d prefer a non-government solution. But is that achievable? Like the rest of healthcare, probably not any time soon.

To the specific, thoughtful points Andrew presents below (welcome any and all thoughts or disagreement - nobody is gonna read all this but I’m posting it anyway):

Drug spending is far less than hospital care & physician services and has stayed fairly consistent for decades

Drugs hold some of the highest margins in healthcare. Yes - Drugmakers deserve to be compensated for ‘riskier’ investment; I am 100% in favor of financial incentives in healthcare - the problem is with the rent seeking behavior I outlined, which I think we agree needs fixing.

You don’t think that high margin drugs influence provider behavior? It’s all inner-connected. e.g., Nonprofit 340B activity (see: arbitrage) and the oncology industry as a couple examples. It’s the same effect that physician compensation has on healthcare. Comp is ~8% of total healthcare spending, and yet compensation contracts incentivizing RVU productivity requirements cause over-utilization of resources and increased downstream healthcare spending. See : private equity activity in healthcare or hospital alignment with physicians (another issue for another day). Same thing with drugs. ADHD medication, opioid crisis as extreme examples. pharmaceutical sales reps in doctors’ offices. PhRMA lobbying dollars. We all love drugs and prescribing them. That’s fine. But need to acknowledge the reality and cascading effects of these practices.

The pie chart omits Part B drug spending - which grew at 9.2% annually from 2008-2021. Higher than inflation by a significant margin

While gross prices are increasing (largely in anticipation of higher PBM rebates), net drug price has actually fallen YoY for the past few years

Rebates & middlemen are obviously a problem, something I’ve touched on in the past but which the current thread doesn’t focus on. Still, list prices are still important to note. Pt. out of pocket costs rise as list prices do. Also affects uninsured. High deductible health plans are a thing. Maybe you can call that bad benefit design, but drugmakers still do it... Lots of patient drug rationing stemming from list prices.

Launch prices of brand new drugs are increasing exponentially consequently. Not factored into list price growth.

Net prices decrease really only after competition is introduced (Humira), which I outline in the original thread.

Drugs improve outcomes & reduce massive downstream hospital costs - how many heart attacks (& associated costs) have statins prevented?

I agree! Drugs (the good kind lol) are amazing and the biggest source of innovation in healthcare. How is the value of a drug determined though? This is where things get fuzzy. Are statins extracting more value than they produce? Do we have empirical evidence to point to that value and is it priced in accordance? I have no idea, you probably do; just questions I’m asking.

Drugs democratize healthcare: health provider services could vary significantly in quality & cost (even in the same hospital!); but if you have insurance and are near a pharmacy, you can get the best drugs in the world

Also agreed! You can get the best drugs in the world…if your formulary covers it, and you have good insurance…or if you can afford the out of pocket list price. Again, this is beyond the scope of the original thread and I acknowledge / agree that middlemen are a problem, probably should have been referenced. But list prices, and launch prices, again, are a problem too.

The vast majority of drugs eventually do go generic and costs plummet. ~90% of scripts are filled with generic drugs - nearly all were once expensive branded drugs. Compare that with every other cost in healthcare, which increases at a higher rate than inflation

The original thread considers pricing gamesmanship, not the fact that generics exist. How are specialty drug cost trends faring? 43% increase in specialty drug costs from 2016-2021. That’s 50% of total drug spend.

Indexing on drug prices alone misses the context that increasingly medicines are low-volume products, targeting niche diseases or produced in small batches - naturally the list price will be higher, but the "N" will be lower to compensate

How can we thoughtfully address drug pricing and objectively obtain the appropriate price of a drug?
How does Medicare or a payor choose to cover and reimburse for these low-volume, extremely high cost, extremely specialized drugs?

Blake brings up the EpiPen, but prior to this innovation, epinephrine injection required a vial & syringe. Anaphylaxis can be very disconcerting for a non-medically trained parent, as they are watching their kid's throat close up. Every second counts - easier & faster dosing is life saving. Mylan also predominantly drove workplace, school & societal education on the value of having an autoinjector on-hand, absolutely saving many lives. Were they personally motivated to do so? Yes - but they also foot the bill. Once they stop, who will pick up that service to ensure we remain adequately supplied for the next emergency?

The level of price gouging involved with EpiPens is akin to surprise billing and the No Surprises Act. It’s predatory behavior on the basis of emergency situations, where pricing is extremely inelastic. It needs to be stocked in schools, day care, with children, with parents, etc.

The bigger story here is that while increasing list prices is perfectly legal, they pursued an anticompetitive price gouging strategy, jacking up the rate by 500+%…and surely we can see something wrong with that. I mean, the feds did.

EpiPen footed a bill for sure - a $345M settlement bill related to EpiPen anticompetitive price fixing.

https://www.reuters.com/business/healthcare-pharmaceuticals/pfizer-agrees-pay-345-mln-resolve-epipen-pricing-lawsuit-2021-07-16/

Along with $264M on the Mylan side

https://www.nytimes.com/2022/02/28/business/viatris-epipen-settlement.html

and another $465M in false claims prior to that

https://www.justice.gov/opa/pr/mylan-agrees-pay-465-million-resolve-false-claims-act-liability-underpaying-epipen-rebates

Don’t get me wrong, these pricing & antitrust dynamics are not beholden to the drug industry - they are widespread, but two wrongs don’t make a right. And obviously we all know pricing and affordability of healthcare is a major issue, especially as the prevalence of high deductible health plans grows.

But it's also worth understanding each individual situation - if a manufacturer takes an "old" drug but spends real R&D money improving it, either via more convenient / less frequent dosing, lower side effects or new indications - they should be rewarded for doing so.

How much did Mylan actually improve the EpiPen? What’s the quantifiable impact of those improvements? A quick Google search tells me that the auto-injector was already developed in the 1970s, but I could be missing something.

To your point, we need to incentivize drugmakers to step in and address generic drug shortages. But raising the EpiPen price 5-fold? Where’s the balance when pharmaceutical companies own the entire market for these drugs?

I am sure you're right that the IRA does a ton of stuff that pharmaceutical investors & firms don't like. But when there are rampant, obvious problems, haven't they kind of made their own bed?

The XLS-30D AMM (Automated Market Maker) Amendment is a proposed update to the XRP Ledger (XRPL) protocol that aims to introduce automated market maker functionality into the XRP Ledger. Here's a more detailed explanation of what this amendment is about:

Automated Market Maker (AMM) Functionality: An AMM is a decentralized financial tool commonly used in the world of cryptocurrencies. It allows users to trade digital assets without the need for a traditional order book or matching engine. Instead, AMMs use smart contracts to automatically facilitate trades and determine asset prices based on supply and demand.

Liquidity Staking Pool: The XLS-30D AMM Amendment plans to create a liquidity staking pool within the XRP Ledger. This means that XRP holders can provide liquidity to this pool by depositing their XRP tokens into it. In return, they receive liquidity pool tokens, which represent their share in the pool.

Earnings and Risk Sharing: Individuals who contribute liquidity to the AMM will have the opportunity to earn passive income. Their earnings will be proportionate to the amount of liquidity they provide to the pool. Additionally, they will share the associated exchange risk with other liquidity providers.

Voting on Trading Fees: XRP liquidity providers can have a say in determining the trading fee within the AMM. The trading fee is typically set based on the proportion of LP (liquidity provider) assets they hold. This feature allows LPs to influence the economics of the AMM.

Community Engagement: The XLS-30D AMM Amendment is designed to engage the XRP community actively. A significant portion of community members have expressed their willingness to participate in AMM liquidity provider services, indicating strong support and participation potential.

Security and Auditing: To ensure the security of this new functionality, the XLS-30D code base underwent a comprehensive audit by the reputable security firm CertiK, which granted it an impressive security score of 95/100. This audit helps address concerns about potential vulnerabilities.

Implementation: However, the implementation of this smart contract functionality hinges on securing an 80% endorsement from XRPL validators. This means that a significant consensus among validators is required to activate the amendment.

In summary, the XLS-30D AMM Amendment is designed to bring automated market maker functionality to the XRP Ledger, allowing XRP holders to earn passive income by participating in liquidity staking pools and influencing trading fees. Business Therapy Series (BTS).. E01

Target Market vs Target Audience 

- Why you should seperate one from the other. 

Case study : Laundry Service Provider

Services: Washing, treatment and ironing  of clothes, plus shoe cleaning.

USP : Home pickup service and delivery after washing, within 48 hours.

Target Market : Corporations, working class professionals in Nigeria.

Target audience : Single/Married, 9-5 working class professionals living in Ikoyi, Chevron, Ikeja GRA, Magodo, Lagos state. (This can be narrowed or broadened, depending on specific objectives, using different filters).

The difference?

Your Target Market is a broad demographic that has the potential to provide your target audience.

On the other hand, your Target Audience are a specific group within your target market to whom you primarily cater to. 

Benefits of specifying your target audience?

1. Efficient resource allocation
2. Improved customer service
3. Specific message delivery
4. Better product development 
5. Higher ROI
6. Competitive advantage 
7. Data driven decisions
8. Brand consistency 
9. Adaptability 
10. Long term growth

You see, identifying a problem is one thing, but the journey towards providing value starts when you're able to Filter the Noise. 
Understanding your primary audience is one of them.

The way healthcare providers navigate payer/insurer coverage policy is completely broken. Today, Penelope Health launches with $100m of committed capital to build the policy intelligence layer that US healthcare never had.

Every medical claim in America lives or dies by payer coverage policies — documents that dictate which codes are covered, which diagnoses qualify, and what documentation is required. There are thousands of these documents which update several times per year and without warning, buried in 50-page PDFs across arcane insurer web portals.

Whereas claims submission got Waystar and Availity, the policy intelligence that sits upstream of every claim has been left to manual portal-trawling, static data vendors, and a lot of Googling.

The result is billions in preventable denials, appeals that take weeks, and clinical staff spending hours on admin that should take seconds.

The problem is harder than it looks. Payers update policies on a random Wednesday and change code coverage overnight. There are 5+ clinically significant differences between any two payer policies on average. And the most important information is routinely hidden in footnotes and appendices — invisible to keyword search.

Penelope Health is the real-time medical coverage policy network that changes all of that with 500,000+ extracted codes, 2 million medical necessity criteria, daily policy updates and sub-second API response times. Query by payer, plan, CPT, ICD or HCPCS — and get back structured, contextual intelligence you can actually act on: claim scrubbing, prior auth generation, appeal letters, payer competitive analysis.

$STLN Q2 2026 earnings: Profitability Reached, but Mix Shift Requires Scrutiny

Starling Oncology delivered a milestone quarter, driving revenue up 34.6% YoY to $161.3M and turning Adjusted EBITDA positive ($229K). The company subsequently raised full-year revenue and gross profit guidance. However, the quality of this revenue is shifting dramatically. High-margin Fee-For-Service (FFS) revenue is shrinking rapidly, forcing the Specialty Pharmacy segment (+58% YoY) and lower-margin Capitated contracts to do all the heavy lifting for the bottom line.

Full article with charts - link in bio

🐂 𝐁𝐮𝐥𝐥 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞
• 𝐏𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐭𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀 𝐌𝐢𝐥𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐨𝐧𝐞 — Adjusted EBITDA flipped to positive $229K from a $4.1M loss a year ago. H1 Free Cash Flow also rebounded powerfully to $9.5M (from negative $14.6M).
• 𝐔𝐧𝐥𝐨𝐜𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐌𝐚𝐬𝐬𝐢𝐯𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐒𝐜𝐚𝐥𝐞 — Achieved exclusivity in California with a major partner, adding 230,000 capitated lives, and signed first delegated contracts outside Florida in Nevada and Oregon.

🐻 𝐁𝐞𝐚𝐫 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐞
• 𝐅𝐞𝐞-𝐅𝐨𝐫-𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐄𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 — FFS revenue dropped 16.7% YoY to $30.8M. This segment's decline acts as a severe drag on Patient Services margins.
• 𝐌𝐋𝐑 𝐒𝐩𝐢𝐤𝐢𝐧𝐠 — The Medical Loss Ratio (MLR) on capitated contracts surged to 85.5% from 71.0% YoY, reflecting the margin pressure of onboarding large, immature patient cohorts.

⚖️ 𝐕𝐞𝐫𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐭: ⚪
Cautiously Bullish. The headline turnaround to positive EBITDA and cash flow is excellent, but investors must monitor the collapsing FFS segment and the spiking MLR to ensure the capitated growth model doesn't destroy gross margins long-term.

𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐓𝐡𝐞𝐦𝐞𝐬

🟢🟢 𝐒𝐩𝐞𝐜𝐢𝐚𝐥𝐭𝐲 𝐏𝐡𝐚𝐫𝐦𝐚𝐜𝐲 𝐢𝐬 𝐭𝐡𝐞 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐰𝐭𝐡 𝐄𝐧𝐠𝐢𝐧𝐞
Accelerating. The Specialty Pharmacy segment remains STLN's most critical financial pillar. Q2 revenue surged 58% YoY to $98.6M, driven by record Part D fills. As new capitated lives are brought onto the platform, STLN is successfully capturing their prescription volumes, providing a massive buffer to overall gross profits.

🟢 𝐂𝐚𝐩𝐢𝐭𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐍𝐞𝐭𝐰𝐨𝐫𝐤 𝐄𝐱𝐩𝐚𝐧𝐬𝐢𝐨𝐧 [NEW]
Accelerating. STLN cemented a major exclusivity deal in California, adding ~230,000 capitated lives. Furthermore, they signed their first delegated contracts in Nevada and Oregon. This resulted in Q2 Capitated Revenue jumping 48.5% YoY to $28.0M.

🔴 𝐅𝐞𝐞-𝐅𝐨𝐫-𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 (𝐅𝐅𝐒) 𝐂𝐨𝐥𝐥𝐚𝐩𝐬𝐞
Decelerating. FFS is STLN's clear laggard. Despite management previously labeling FFS declines as 'minor cannibalization', Q2 FFS revenue plunged 16.7% YoY to $30.8M (worsening from a 10% decline in Q1). Because FFS natively carries higher margins, its erosion directly pressures Patient Services gross profitability.

🔴 𝐌𝐞𝐝𝐢𝐜𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐑𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨 (𝐌𝐋𝐑) 𝐒𝐩𝐢𝐤𝐞𝐬 𝐨𝐧 𝐍𝐞𝐰 𝐂𝐨𝐡𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐬
Reversing. STLN's MLR on capitated contracts shot up to 85.5% in Q2, compared to 71.0% a year ago. Direct costs for capitated patients surged 78.7% YoY, significantly outpacing the 48.5% revenue growth. While management expects newly delegated contracts to run higher initially, this exact data point contradicts the narrative of effortless margin expansion.

🟢 𝐒𝐭𝐚𝐫𝐥𝐢𝐧𝐠 𝐍𝐞𝐱𝐮𝐬 𝐏𝐨𝐫𝐭𝐚𝐥 𝐋𝐚𝐮𝐧𝐜𝐡 [NEW]
Scheduled for mid-August, the proprietary 'Starling Nexus' provider portal aims to tighten clinical pathway adherence among network physicians. If successful, this technology will directly pull down the elevated MLR and could facilitate higher Part D prescription capture for the pharmacy segment.

🔴 𝐌𝐚𝐜𝐫𝐨: 𝐓𝐚𝐫𝐢𝐟𝐟 𝐚𝐧𝐝 𝐓𝐫𝐚𝐝𝐞 𝐕𝐮𝐥𝐧𝐞𝐫𝐚𝐛𝐢𝐥𝐢𝐭𝐲
Management explicitly warned in their Safe Harbor language that their outlook assumes a stable global market, noting the business would be 'negatively impacted if recent tariff rate increases and exchange rate changes persist'. Given their reliance on specialized oncology drugs, supply chain inflation remains a looming macro risk.

𝐎𝐭𝐡𝐞𝐫 𝐊𝐏𝐈𝐬

𝐇𝟏 𝐅𝐫𝐞𝐞 𝐂𝐚𝐬𝐡 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐰: $9.5 million
Reversing. FCF improved massively from a cash burn of $(14.6)M in H1 2025. This was driven by a $24.9M YoY swing in operating cash flow, validating management's prior quarter claims that scale is allowing them to negotiate significantly better vendor and drug procurement terms.

𝐂𝐨𝐧𝐬𝐨𝐥𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭: $27.2 million
Accelerating. Up 55.2% YoY, vastly outpacing top-line revenue growth of 34.6%. This indicates that despite the MLR spike in patient services, the volume leverage and margin profile of the Specialty Pharmacy segment are more than compensating at the consolidated level.

𝐆𝐮𝐢𝐝𝐚𝐧𝐜𝐞

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐑𝐞𝐯𝐞𝐧𝐮𝐞: $650 to $670 million
Accelerating. Raised from the previous range of $630-$650 million. The midpoint ($660M) implies continued high-growth momentum, fueled by the newly announced 230k California lives and Nevada/Oregon expansion.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐆𝐫𝐨𝐬𝐬 𝐏𝐫𝐨𝐟𝐢𝐭: $105 to $110 million
Accelerating. Raised from the prior $97-$107 million range. Suggests management confidence that the Pharmacy margins will hold up and that newly added capitated cohorts will mature and improve their MLR in the second half of the year.

𝐅𝐘𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $2 to $7 million
Stable. The range was updated from $0-$9 million. While the floor was raised, the ceiling was lowered, keeping the implied midpoint essentially flat at $4.5 million. This reflects near-term onboarding costs and the MLR drag of integrating the massive new California exclusivity deal.

𝐐𝟑 𝟐𝟎𝟐𝟔 𝐀𝐝𝐣𝐮𝐬𝐭𝐞𝐝 𝐄𝐁𝐈𝐓𝐃𝐀: $500K to $1.5M
Accelerating. A sequential step-up from Q2's $229K, as the company absorbs the ramp-up of Florida delegated lives.

𝐊𝐞𝐲 𝐐𝐮𝐞𝐬𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧𝐬

𝐅𝐞𝐞-𝐅𝐨𝐫-𝐒𝐞𝐫𝐯𝐢𝐜𝐞 𝐅𝐥𝐨𝐨𝐫
With Fee-For-Service revenue declining nearly 17% year-over-year, where does management see the natural floor for this segment, and how much is true cannibalization versus lost market share?

𝐌𝐋𝐑 𝐌𝐚𝐭𝐮𝐫𝐚𝐭𝐢𝐨𝐧 𝐂𝐮𝐫𝐯𝐞
